questions.question: Science classes name six forms of energy: light, heat, sound, electrical, chemical and mechanical energy. What do scientists mean by energy?
questions.answer: The ability to do work or cause change
choices: The ability to do work or cause change
A push or a pull that acts on an object
A fuel that is burned to give off heat
A kind of matter that takes up space
questions.context: Energy is the ability to do work or cause change: to move something, warm it, light it up or make it sound. A push or a pull is a force, not energy, and fuels such as wood and coal are matter that stores energy, not energy itself.
questions.grade_note: Grade 3-5 energy lessons (Teach Engineering) and Virginia's grade 5 standard SOL 5.2 open with energy as the ability to do work or cause change.

questions.question: A flashlight lies switched off in a drawer with a new battery inside. In what form does the battery store its energy?
questions.context: A battery stores its energy as chemical energy, in the substances packed inside it. Only when the flashlight is switched on does the battery change that chemical energy into electrical energy, which flows through the wires to the bulb.
questions.grade_note: Texas's grade 5 standard TEKS 5.8A uses this very example: a flashlight battery's chemical energy changes into electrical energy and then light.

questions.question: A flashlight's bulb takes in electrical energy from the battery and shines into the dark. What does the bulb change that electrical energy into?
questions.context: Every bulb gives off some heat along with its light. An old-style bulb with a glowing wire turns most of its energy into heat; a modern light-emitting diode (LED) wastes far less, but it still warms up.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.8A lessons trace a flashlight's energy into light and a little thermal energy, and name the belief that light is the only energy a flashlight makes.

questions.question: A desk fan blows air across a stuffy bedroom on a hot summer night. What energy change happens inside the fan's motor?
questions.context: An electric motor changes electrical energy into mechanical energy, the energy of motion, and that spins the blades. A generator does the opposite, turning motion into electrical energy, and a car's engine turns the chemical energy in gasoline into motion.
questions.grade_note: The grade 5 curriculum line for TEKS 5.8A names electrical energy changing into motion in a fan as an everyday energy chain.

questions.question: Inside a phone, a caller's voice arrives as an electrical signal. Which part of the phone changes that electrical energy into sound?
questions.context: A speaker changes electrical energy into sound by making a small cone shake back and forth very fast. The microphone does the opposite job, changing the owner's own voice into an electrical signal; the battery supplies electrical energy, and the screen changes it into light.
questions.grade_note: The grade 5 curriculum line for TEKS 5.8A names electrical energy changing into sound in a speaker as an everyday energy chain.

questions.question: Solar panels on a school roof run its lamps and computers on sunny days. What energy change happens inside the panels?
questions.context: A solar panel changes sunlight straight into electrical energy, with no heating step. Heat does not help it: a panel works a little worse when it is hot, and a cold, bright day suits it well.
questions.grade_note: Light changing into electrical energy in a solar panel is a standard example in grade 5 energy lessons (Kesler Science's TEKS 5.8A lesson).

questions.question: Wind turns the sails of a windmill, and coal burns in a power plant to make electricity. Where did nearly all the energy in the wind and the coal first come from?
questions.context: The Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly, and that sets the air moving as wind; Earth's spinning only bends the wind's path. Coal formed from ancient plants that stored the Sun's energy. Earth's inner heat and the Moon's pull on the tides are real energy sources too, but tiny beside the Sun.
questions.grade_note: The unit's grade 5 scope teaches that most energy on Earth comes from the Sun, as CK-12's Earth Science (almost all energy comes from the Sun) and Energy Kids (wind from the Sun's uneven heating) do.

questions.question: At a big dam, water rushes down through huge pipes and spins giant wheels. What form of energy in the rushing water makes the wheels turn?
questions.context: Anything that moves has mechanical energy, and rushing water carries a great deal of it. The water holds no electricity: the spinning wheels, called turbines, drive generators that change the mechanical energy into electrical energy.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 benchmark SC.5.P.10.1 names mechanical energy among the basic forms, taught as the energy of motion.

questions.question: Four everyday things each hold energy, and each holds a different form of it. Which one holds chemical energy?
choices: A stone warmed by a fire
questions.context: Food stores chemical energy, which the body releases to move and to keep warm; wood, coal, gasoline and batteries store it too. The wound-up spring stores mechanical energy, the warm stone holds thermal energy and the ringing bell gives off sound energy.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 benchmark SC.5.P.10.1 lists chemical energy among the basic forms, taught as energy stored in food, fuel and batteries.
